question: A support message has just been classified. What is the next step?
answers: Send the draft reply to the customer
Retrain the model on the message
Fetch help articles and order details
Close the ticket without a reply
fact: After classifying, tool calls fetch the relevant help articles and the customer's order record, so the drafting model works from real facts instead of memory.

question: In a support flow, where does the stronger model earn its cost?
answers: Drafting the reply from fetched facts
Sorting messages by topic
Looking up the order record
Counting tickets for the team dashboard
fact: Routing and lookups are cheap steps. The stronger model is saved for drafting, where tone and reasoning over the retrieved sources matter most.

question: A retailer's customer writes about a billing dispute and mentions a lawyer. What should the assistant do?
answers: Send the draft reply automatically
Ask the customer to rephrase
Close it as out of scope
Pass it to a person with the draft
fact: Sensitive cases go to a person, with the draft and sources attached. The assistant saves time, but a human still makes the call.

question: Which set of measures best judges a support assistant?
answers: Tokens used, reply length and uptime
Resolution, accuracy and satisfaction
Model size, speed and cost per token
Chats opened, logins and page views
fact: Track how many cases it resolves, its accuracy on a fixed set of real tickets, and customer satisfaction. Compare all three with a baseline from before launch.

question: A support bot passes its tests but customers report wrong refund dates. Likeliest gap?
answers: The eval set missed real refund cases
The classifier model is far too small
The replies are not long enough
The context window is too large
fact: An eval set must mirror real tickets, including awkward ones. Tests built from tidy examples flatter the bot and hide the failures customers actually meet.

question: Staff want HR answers from policies kept in SharePoint. What is the quickest first step?
answers: Build a vector database
Move policies into a new wiki
Fine-tune a model on the files
Connect SharePoint to ChatGPT
fact: ChatGPT Enterprise connectors link to apps like SharePoint and Drive and generally follow each user's existing access, so many internal assistants need no custom build.

question: Why show a source link beside each answer from an internal assistant?
answers: It makes the reply arrive much faster
Staff can check the policy themselves
It trains the model on the link
It hides outdated pages
fact: Citations let a person open the policy and verify the answer. That builds trust and makes wrong or stale answers easy to spot and report.

question: An IT help assistant quotes a retired VPN guide. Who keeps content like this fresh?
answers: The model itself, as it keeps learning
Whoever built the first prototype
Named content owners with review dates
The security team, once a year
fact: A model does not update itself from your files. Each source needs a named owner and review date, with the index refreshed whenever a document changes.

question: A logistics firm reads supplier invoices with AI. What happens right after the file is read?
answers: Fields are extracted in a fixed format
The invoice is paid straight away
A person retypes the totals
The model is retrained on that invoice
fact: Structured outputs make the model return supplier, date and totals in a set shape, such as JSON, so later steps and systems can use them without guessing.

question: Extracted invoice totals do not match the line items. Which step should catch this?
answers: A longer prompt before extraction
The payment run itself
Rules that check the extracted fields
Monthly retraining of the whole model
fact: Plain code rules, such as totals adding up, a known supplier and no duplicate number, check the model's output. Anything that fails is held back.

question: An invoice fails a validation rule. Where should it go?
answers: Straight into the finance system
An exception queue for a person
Back to the model until it passes
Back to the supplier by email
fact: Looping until it passes can hide real errors. A person reviews the exception, and fixed cases are worth adding to the eval set.

question: Extraction is 97% right overall, but most errors hit the payment amount. What next?
answers: Accept it, since 97% is high
Switch every field to manual entry
Raise the context window size
Add stricter checks on that field
fact: Overall accuracy hides costly mistakes. Measure per field, then add rule checks or a person where an error costs money, and relax elsewhere.

question: A rep wants account research before a call. Which ChatGPT feature fits?
answers: Deep research with connectors
Fine-tuning on past emails
A realtime voice model for calls
The Batch API
fact: Deep research produces a sourced, multi-source report, and connectors can bring in the rep's own CRM, calendar and documents. A human still checks the claims.

question: How would you judge a sales team's ChatGPT rollout?
answers: Number of prompts typed per rep
Seats purchased compared with plan
Time saved and weekly active users
Pages of proposals produced a week
fact: Pick a baseline task such as proposal hours, then measure time saved and adoption. Seats bought and volume produced are weak proxies; low use predicts a weak renewal.

question: A rep saves AI call summaries into the CRM. Where should a person check?
answers: The spelling in the full transcript
Actions and commitments before saving
Nothing, since summaries are factual
The length of the summary text
fact: Summaries can drop or invent actions, dates and figures. A quick check by the rep before saving keeps the CRM, and any later email, trustworthy.

question: Which engineering team suits a first Codex rollout?
answers: A team with no tests or reviews
A brand new product with no code
The whole company at once
One with a clear backlog of tasks
fact: Land Codex where a visible backlog exists, so wins are easy to see. Measure cycle time and pull requests merged, then widen to other teams.

question: Why do tests matter when Codex changes code?
answers: They show if a change broke something
They make Codex write its code faster
They replace the code review
They teach Codex the house style
fact: Tests are the safety net: Codex can run them and a person reviews the change. Passing tests lower the risk but do not replace review.

question: Why give a text-to-SQL assistant read-only database access?
answers: It makes the queries run faster
It stops the model guessing joins
A bad query cannot change data
It lets the model reach more tables
fact: Read-only rights mean a wrong or hostile query can at worst return a bad answer, not edit or delete records. Pair it with a governed warehouse and least privilege.

question: Two teams define 'active customer' differently, so answers clash. What helps?
answers: A larger model for the questions
A metric layer both teams use
A longer system prompt on top
Letting each user choose a meaning
fact: A metric layer holds agreed definitions, such as what counts as active, so the model uses them instead of guessing. Wrong definitions often cause wrong data answers.

question: Showing the SQL behind a data answer proves the numbers are right.
fact: The query lets an analyst check joins and filters, which helps catch errors. It does not prove correctness; a wrong join can still look tidy.

question: In contract review against a playbook, what does the model do first?
answers: Rewrites the whole contract
Decides whether the firm signs
Emails the other side's lawyer
Pulls out clauses to compare
fact: The model extracts key clauses, compares each with the firm's playbook of accepted positions and flags gaps. A lawyer reviews the flags and signs off.

question: Why should each contract flag cite the clause it came from?
answers: The lawyer can jump to the text
It lowers the token cost
It teaches the playbook
It lets the model skip reading
fact: A citation lets the lawyer check a flag against the actual wording in seconds. Without it, review means rereading everything or trusting the tool.

question: A contract lacks an expected clause and the tool reports no issues. What control helps?
answers: A higher temperature setting
Reviewing shorter contracts first
A checklist of required clauses
A larger context window
fact: Missing clauses are easy to overlook. Give the tool an explicit list of required clauses and test it on contracts known to omit them.

question: What is a latency budget in a voice agent?
answers: A monthly spending cap on all calls
Time allowed for each step of a turn
The longest call length permitted
The number of callers handled at once
fact: A voice turn chains listening, the model, any tool lookups and speech. The budget splits a target delay across them; one slow lookup can break the flow.

question: A caller says 'let me speak to someone'. What should the voice agent do?
answers: Ask three more questions first
End the call politely
Offer to read the terms aloud
Hand over with a short summary
fact: Hand off at once and pass the context, so the caller does not repeat themselves. Pushing someone to stay with the bot damages trust.

question: Why keep transcripts of voice agent calls?
answers: To check quality and settle disputes
To make the voice sound much warmer
To cut down the delay in replies
To avoid asking callers for consent
fact: Transcripts support quality review, evals and audit. Storing them brings privacy duties: tell callers, limit retention and mask sensitive details.

question: A telco voice agent must not quote plans it does not know. What enforces that?
answers: Tell it in the prompt to be careful
Fetch plan data; hand off if absent
Train callers to speak clearly
Give it a warmer voice
fact: Prompts alone can slip. Keep the agent inside its script by letting it quote only plan data fetched by a tool, and hand off when nothing is found.

question: An IT-ticket agent reset the wrong password. What helps you trace what happened?
answers: A longer system prompt for it
The agent's own final summary
The chat window history shown
An audit log of each tool call
fact: An audit log records what acted, when and with which inputs. The agent's own summary is not a record, and logs let you review and reverse actions.

question: A refund agent approved a payment in error. What design makes it easiest to fix?
answers: Reversible actions plus rollback
A bigger model making each approval
Telling the agent to be careful
Faster approvals with no waiting
fact: Make actions undoable where you can, such as a held or reversible refund, and add approval for one-way steps. Rollback turns a mistake into a small fix.

question: Evals show routine refunds are reliable. Which approval rule fits?
answers: A person still approves every refund
Auto-approve if the model feels sure
Agent does small; a person okays large
Review after customers complain
fact: Use risk tiers: let the agent act alone on small, routine refunds where evals are strong, and keep a person for large or unusual ones. Review the tiers as evidence grows.

question: What does giving an agent its own scoped identity allow?
answers: Letting it sign in as any employee
Making its answers more accurate
Skipping the later security review
Limiting and watching its access
fact: In Frontier, each agent gets its own identity with scoped permissions tied to the company's identity systems, plus monitoring, so its access is limited and reviewable.

question: A 600-person firm wants drafting and research help for staff, with no developers. Best fit?
answers: A custom app on the API
ChatGPT Enterprise
Codex seats
A fine-tuned model
fact: Enterprise is the sales-led plan for knowledge workers, with admin and security controls. The API suits teams building their own apps, which this firm cannot staff.

question: A bank's workflow must send identifiable customer data to a model. Which route fits?
answers: API behind a gateway with masking
Staff paste the data into ChatGPT
ChatGPT Enterprise on its own
Upload files to a shared Project
fact: Identifiable data in automated workflows usually calls for the API with a customer-side gateway that masks and re-identifies. Each route unlocks a different class of data.

question: Trying a ready-made tool before building custom code is a sensible default.
fact: Buy before build: a connector, Project or Skill often solves the problem in days. Build on the API when scale, many systems or a custom screen make it necessary.

question: A customer wants one assistant over eight systems, with logins, for 20,000 users. Best fit?
answers: A shared Project
A single Skill
A custom build on the API
A larger Project with more files
fact: Many systems, many users and a custom screen with permissions are the signs to build on the API. A Project or Skill suits a team, not a product.

question: When is a connector enough, rather than custom RAG?
answers: Millions of files need special ranking
Answers must appear in a customer app
Search needs exact part-code matching
Content sits in connected apps
fact: If the content is in apps like Drive or SharePoint, connectors give grounded answers with no build. Go custom for huge archives, special search or customer-facing apps.

question: At a mid-market firm, who usually builds and owns an API-based assistant?
answers: OpenAI's account team after the sale
Their engineers and a business owner
Their finance team, as budget holder
One ChatGPT admin in the IT team
fact: The customer's engineers build and run it, a named business owner is accountable for results, and OpenAI or a partner advises. Mid-market teams often lack capacity, so ask early.

question: When should a seller bring in a solutions engineer?
answers: When security or integration is deep
After the contract has been signed off
When the customer first complains
At the final round of price talks
fact: A seller owns the plan and the relationship, but brings in a solutions engineer before promising detail on security, residency or integration. Saying so builds trust.

question: When do forward deployed engineers fit best?
answers: Each small ChatGPT seat purchase
Simple setup of a shared Project
Complex, high-value agent builds
Routine password reset requests
fact: FDEs embed with a customer to get agents into production. Mid-market firms may get limited FDE time, so ask how it is allocated and do not promise it.

question: A customer asks if they need ChatGPT Enterprise or the API. Which question splits it best?
answers: How many tokens will you use?
Which cloud provider do you use?
Is your data in a warehouse?
Staff use, or an app or automation?
fact: Enterprise serves people using ChatGPT for their work; the API serves products and automated workflows. Many customers land on one and expand to the other.

question: What is routing in an AI workflow?
answers: Sending a request down the right path
Shortening requests into fewer words
Storing replies for later reuse
Encrypting messages in transit
fact: A cheap model or rule labels the request, then it goes down the right path: a small model for easy cases, a stronger one for hard ones, a person for risky ones.

question: Why split a long task into steps rather than one big prompt?
answers: Steps remove the need for evals
Each step is easier to test and fix
Chained steps cost less in total
Smaller prompts avoid tool errors
fact: Steps such as classify, retrieve, draft and check can each be evaluated alone, so you can see where a failure starts. One huge prompt hides the cause.

question: In 'classify then act', what decides the next step?
answers: The length of the message
The time of day it arrived
The label given to the request
The age of the customer account
fact: The classification label is the switch: billing goes one way, delivery another, complaints to a person. Wrong labels send cases the wrong way, so test the classifier.

question: In 'extract, validate, act', which check is most dependable?
answers: The model rating its own confidence
A second, longer prompt
A shorter limit on output length
Fixed rules written as code
fact: Code rules behave the same every time and are easy to test, such as totals adding up or dates being valid. A model's self-rated confidence is a weaker guard.

question: Where should a human approval step sit in a workflow?
answers: After the action has already been run
Just before a risky or one-way action
At the very start of every single case
On each harmless, read-only lookup step
fact: Put the gate just before the step that is hard to undo, such as paying, sending or deleting. Reading and drafting can run freely, which keeps the person's workload small.

question: The classifier cannot place a message in any known category. What then?
answers: Send it to a person's queue
Force the closest category
Ignore the message
Ask the model to guess again
fact: Have a fallback for the unknown: unmatched or low-quality cases go to a person. The share that falls through is a useful metric and shows where to improve.

question: A payment call times out and the workflow retries. What stops a double payment?
answers: A faster timer between the retries
A bigger model handling the retry
A unique key for each action
A prompt telling it not to repeat
fact: Give each action a unique key. If a retry arrives with the same key, the system sees it already ran and does not do it twice. In plain words, retrying becomes safe.

question: An auditor asks why a claim was auto-approved. What answers it?
answers: The model's own later explanation
The latest version of the prompt
A screenshot of today's dashboard
Logged inputs, sources, decision
fact: Log the inputs, retrieved sources, model version, output and who approved. A model's explanation written afterwards is not a record of what actually happened.

question: Which job suits real time rather than batch?
answers: Overnight extraction of invoices
A live chat with a waiting user
Drafting the monthly board report
Re-tagging a ten-year-old archive
fact: If nobody is waiting, batch is cheaper through discounted processing. If a person is waiting, you need real time and must watch latency.

question: A pipeline classifies, retrieves, drafts and checks. Quality fell after a prompt edit. Best first move?
answers: Run the evals on each step alone
Rerun the whole flow and hope
Swap to the oldest model
Add another step at the end
fact: Step-level evals show which stage got worse, so you fix that stage instead of guessing. Keep prompts versioned so an edit can be undone.

question: In a pilot-to-production path, what is the prototype's job?
answers: Prove the finished system is secure
Serve all customers from launch day
Show the idea can work on real tasks
Stand in for a proper eval set
fact: A prototype is quick and cheap. Evals on real data, security review, a limited rollout with monitoring and then scale follow; skipping steps is where pilots fail.

question: A telco is picking its first workflow. Which is the best choice?
answers: Cancelling contracts from chat
Rare VIP complaint handling
Diagnosing network faults live
Triage of bill queries
fact: Pick by volume, risk and checkability: frequent bill queries give savings, are easy to check and carry low risk. Rare or one-way tasks make weak first proofs.

question: A pilot should record a baseline, such as minutes per ticket, before it starts.
fact: Without a baseline you cannot show what changed. Measure time per task, volume and error rate first, then compare after the pilot against agreed criteria.

question: A security review begins after a pilot succeeds and delays launch. Lesson?
answers: Skip it while still a pilot
Start it early, in parallel
Run it after launch day
Leave it to the vendor alone
fact: Late security review is a classic blocker. Send security documents up front and run the review alongside the business evaluation, so it does not stall launch.

question: A hospital group's pilot worked well but no team will take it live. What was missing?
answers: A business owner for the outcome
A larger context window in the model
A fine-tuned version of the model
A faster supplier of graphics chips
fact: No named owner is a common blocker. Someone in the business must own the result, the budget and the decision on what a person approves.

question: What should monitoring watch in a retailer's limited rollout?
answers: Logins, screen time and page views
Rival prices and press coverage
Quality, cost and handoff rate
Seat price, discounts and term
fact: Track answer quality on sampled cases, cost per task and how often cases go to a person. Rising handoffs or falling quality are early warnings.

question: Which pair of measures fits a document-processing workflow?
answers: Resolution rate and satisfaction
Cycle time and pull requests merged
Weekly active users and seats used
Field accuracy and no-touch rate
fact: Measure each use case on its own terms. Documents: field accuracy and the share processed with no human touch. Support: resolution and satisfaction. Codex: cycle time.

question: A regional bank wants KYC document review. Which shape fits?
answers: A chatbot that opens accounts alone
Extract, validate, officer approves
Fine-tuning on past customer files
Staff pasting files into a chat
fact: KYC is extract, validate and send exceptions to an officer, who decides. Customer data may need masking and a residency check, so involve security early.

question: A regional insurer's customers mix Malay and English in one message. What first?
answers: Test on real mixed-language messages
Translate everything to English first
Use one formal Malay sample
Test only the shortest messages
fact: Mixing languages in one message is common in ASEAN. Test on real chats per language, and costs may differ because token counts vary by language.

question: Pilot users liked the tool but weekly use fell after month two. What first?
answers: Buy more seats to widen the reach
Swap to a newer, bigger model now
Find which workflows have stalled
End the pilot and move on early
fact: Falling use is a warning for renewal. Ask which workflows stalled, then fix with champions, role-specific training and shared prompts or Skills.
